overview: Ancient Egypt brought together royal power, skilled workshops and a durable written culture along the Nile. Its art changed substantially across the Old and Middle Kingdoms. Pyramids, family memorials and ordinary letters reveal different parts of that society; surviving evidence is often weighted toward elite tombs.

items.text: At Saqqara, Djoser's Step Pyramid formed the center of a complex of stone buildings and underground chambers. Later builders developed smooth-sided pyramids.
Papyrus sheets were made by layering strips of the stalk's inner pith and drying them under pressure. Sheets could be joined into writing rolls.
Old Kingdom tomb chapels depicted food offerings and agricultural work. These images were meant to sustain the dead, so they are more than documentary pictures of daily life.
Middle Kingdom jewelers placed tiny inlays on ornaments and sometimes decorated their backs with elaborate chasing, visible principally to their wearers.
Unis had religious spells carved inside his pyramid late in Dynasty 5. Later kings, and eventually queens, also received these Pyramid Texts.
Middle Kingdom memorials increasingly pictured extended families and associates. Such monuments show religious commemoration reaching beyond the ruler alone.
Papyrus carried accounts, letters and legal agreements as well as religious works. Black ink usually supplied the main text; red ink could mark emphasis.
The same marsh plant also supplied material for baskets, sandals, ropes and small boats. A writing technology belonged to a much wider craft economy.
